articles.title: The Best MicroSD Express Cards for Nintendo Switch 2 Right Now
articles.summary: The Switch 2 needs a different type of SD card than usual to expand storage: the microSD Express card.
articles.body:
The Nintendo Switch 2 has been out for almost a year now, and while Nintendo seems a little disappointed with its sales, it was still the best-selling console of of 2025. If you're one of the many people who has grabbed a Switch 2 in the last year you've probably noticed that it doesn't quite have enough storage, with only 256GB of space to fit all your games onto that console. Luckily that storage is expandable, but you will need a special MicroSD Express card to do it. And, well, they're more expensive than regular SD cards.

The Best MicroSD Express Cards for Switch 2 Right Now

MicroSD Express cards have been around for a while, but there were still only a few on the market as creative professionals haven’t really found much of a use for them. Now, with the Switch 2 launch, there's been a deluge of new Express cards to fill that gap.

My colleagues and I are continuously testing these cards – including that super cheap Walmart-brand one, which is fine – but if we were to recommend any based on experience, these are the MicroSD Express cards (an essential Switch 2 accessory !) we'd say to buy right now. These come from reputable manufacturers that have a track record of making excellent storage expansion cards. We'll be updating this as we play around with the Switch 2 and SD cards.

Unlike many devices, the Nintendo Switch 2 is mandating a MicroSD Express card for storage expansion. Nintendo hasn’t really explained its reasoning behind the decision, but it’s not hard to see why it might want to require faster storage.

For one, the flash storage built into the system is the same kind of UFS flash that powers most smartphones . This storage is much faster than the eMMC drive in the original Switch, and it’s likely Nintendo wanted its developers to be able to count on that kind of storage speed, no matter if the game is being stored internally or on an expansion card.

The only thing you can use a regular old MicroSD card for is loading screenshots and videos you took on your first-gen Switch. That means unlike something like the PS5, which allows you to store last-generation games on slower external drives, Nintendo isn’t allowing for any wiggle room here. If you want to expand the Nintendo Switch 2 storage, you’re going to need a MicroSD Express card.

The Lexar Play Pro is the fastest and most capacious card available. Supporting read times up to 900MB/s and storage space up to 1TB, this is handily the best MicroSD Express card out there right now. After a few months of wobbly stock issues, you can now more reliably find this card out in the wild at the typical retailers. Unfortunately, it is quite expensive. But if you do want the best SD card for your Switch 2, it’s worth investing in the Lexar Play Pro for a fast card that won't degrade quickly.

Samsung P9 MicroSD Express Card – Photos

MicroSD Express cards have been out long enough now that we're starting to see more affordable cards from some of the biggest brands. While it's not quite as cheap as the Onn MicroSD Express card you can buy from Walmart, this Samsung card is extremely affordable for what it is. At the time of writing, you can get a 256GB version of the card for $32, while the 512GB version is a bit more expensive, at $99.

There are some caveats to this one, of course. While we found in our testing that the Samsung P9 MicroSD Express card has solid sequential read and write times, it lacks a bit when it comes to random read and write speeds. What that means is that you can copy your games over to this SD card super fast, but it's not going to have the fastest load times. That doesn't mean the load times aren't fast, though; we were able to load up Donkey Kong Bananza in 21 seconds and Tears of the Kingdom in 9 seconds. So while there are faster cards out there, you're only really losing out on a second here and there.

But for most people who just want reliable expansion storage for their Switch 2 that's not going to break the bank, you can't really go wrong with the Samsung P9. It's not the absolute cheapest on the market, but you can bet it'll last a lot longer than that Onn card.

I have so many SanDisk SD cards lying around, and that shouldn’t be super surprising. Over the years, SanDisk has become one of the most prolific SD card manufacturers, and now it has a MicroSD Express card. Unlike the Lexar version, SanDisk doesn’t have a fancy name for its card. Though this card does come in a 512GB-capacity version now, 256GB would mirror the internal storage of the Nintendo Switch 2.

Still, doubling your storage isn’t a bad deal, especially if you can find this card at a lower price. It’s also not quite as fast as the Lexar Play Pro, coming in with a read speed of up to 880MB/s. That’s a minor enough disparity that you’re not going to notice any difference when you’re loading up Mario Kart World , but 20MB/s is still 20MB/s.

The Best (and Only) Official MicroSD Express Card

Samsung’s MicroSD Express card is the one that’s being sold directly by Nintendo, which definitely gives it some weight. Since it came out back in May, Samsung has released its actual speeds and feeds. This MicroSD card gets 800MB/s of read speeds, which doesn't make it the fastest SD card here, but it'll still load games plenty fast. Plus, it has Mario on the retail packaging, so that's a bonus, right?

The card does come with a three-year warranty, but Samsung only offers it in a 256GB size. That basically doubles the initial storage of the Switch 2, but it would still be nice to see a 512GB or 1TB option for true game archival – especially as it's the official option.

At the end of the day, it being the "official" MicroSD Express card for the Switch 2 doesn't mean much. It might have received Nintendo's seal of approval, but this MicroSD card isn't going to be much different than any other card on this list, at least beyond the red paint job.

While it would be nice to be able to say something like "a MicroSD Express card is a MicroSD Express card," they're not all created equal. More premium cards will be able to transmit data more efficiently, while cheaper cards are obviously going to slow down a bit. But when we're talking about a 512GB SD card that is 40% cheaper than the same size option from Lexar, a slower speed might just be worth it.

Onn is Walmart's budget tech brand, and that should set some expectations right out of the gate. In fact, when we reviewed the Onn 512GB MicroSD Express card , we found that while the Nintendo Switch 2 worked with no issues, it had data transfer speeds that were a bit slower than the console's native storage. That sounds bad, and it's not great , but at the end of the day that's only going to result in another second or so added to transfer times here and there. Definitely not the end of the world.

But what was surprising about this Onn card was that it was reliable, which is where I typically expect budget storage devices to fall flat. Throughout our testing process, performance stayed steady rather than running into the same issues that the PNY 128GB MicroSD Express card ran into. Of course, like any SD card, it'll likely degrade over time, but as long as you're not looking for long-term game archival, it'll get the job done.

While the 256GB that the Nintendo Switch 2 has is paltry, it might be enough if you only play a few games every year. However, if you're the type of gamer that needs to install everything that comes out, even if you only play it for five minutes – you know who you are – you're going to need quite a bit more space.

Unfortunately with the special storage standard the Switch 2 requires, large-capacity MicroSD Express cards can be quite expensive. Getting an affordable 256GB MicroSD Express card will double your storage, which should be plenty for most people. But if you want a lot of buffer room, I'd recommend a 512GB card just to be on the safe side.

Or you could just go all out and get 1TB of storage. That'll be expensive, but you'll probably never have to think about Switch 2 storage space ever again. Only the most archival-obsessed people need something like that, but, again, you know who you are .

SD Express is theoretically much faster than older SD cards, and that largely comes down to how it interfaces with the device. Rather than connecting to a bespoke SD card interface, SD Express uses PCI Express 3.1, which is what SSDs use on PC.

Don’t go expecting a MicroSD Express card to be as fast as the NVMe SSDs in handheld gaming PCs , though. While the full-sized SD Express cards can come close, with read speeds up to 3,940MB/s, the MicroSD Express cards can only hit a maximum of 985MB/s. Still, that’s much faster than the older MicroSD cards used by the original Nintendo Switch.

How long will a MicroSD Express card last?

Just like any SD card, MicroSD Express cards aren’t meant to be used for long-term data storage, and so they have a shelf life. How long they’ll last depends largely on the environment it's being used in and whether or not you’re dropping it. I wouldn’t expect a MicroSD Express card to last more than 5-10 years before it needs to be replaced, so be sure to keep anything important backed up.

How hard is it to install a MicroSD Express card?

Once you actually have a MicroSD Express card, it's relatively easy to upgrade your Switch 2 storage . Make sure your console is off, and then open the kickstand at the back of the console, and look along the bottom for a small MicroSD Card slot, where you can insert the extra storage. You can check out IGN's comprehensive guide to installing a MicroSD Express card for more details.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering Hobbit Gift Bundles Are Back in Stock at Amazon
articles.summary: Save almost 20% and get a Collector Booster included with 9 Play Boosters, too.
articles.body:
In case you missed it, Magic: The Gathering has returned to Middle-Earth with some gusto. The Lord of the Rings set is widely regarded as one of the best Universes Beyond offerings yet, and The Hobbit is getting a pretty great reception from players, too.

As the set only launched recently, its Collector Boosters are harder to find than the Arkenstone in Smaug’s hoard of treasures, but Amazon has a “deal” that might get your attention.

There Is A Catch, Depending On Where You Stand

We say “deal” because, as with many things with this set right now, the Magic: The Gathering Hobbit Gift bundle is being sold for more than its MSRP.

In fact, Wizards says it should be $89.99, so $164 is a colossal price hike. And yet, the same bundle can be found for $200 elsewhere, or is simply sold out with no sign of returning.

We’re giving you this information up front because you’re a big Hobbit now and you can spend your money as you please, but this is still a discount of 18% on the same bundle purchased elsewhere. If you really want it, buy it; if you don’t want to spend that kind of money, we get it, but at least you’re informed.

So what’s the big draw? While it is true that you get 9 Play Boosters inside, the most valuable cards in the set are restricted to Collector Boosters. And in this bundle, you’ll find one (hopefully to rule them all).

Smaug, Wicked Worm (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

Bard, King of Dale (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

Thorin, Mountain-king (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

Thranduil, the Elvenking (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

The Queen of Dale (Showcase) (Surge Foil)

Gandalf, Goblins' Bane (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

The Arkenstone (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

Smaug the Magnificent (Showcase) (Surge Foil)

Gleaming Splendor (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

Smaug? Bard? Gandalf? What’ll it be? Well, that’s the point, really: you could open a whole bunch of neat rare cards, or you could pay your next month’s rent by pulling a Gleaming Splendor.

Aside from the ten total packs, you’ll also get 34 land cards that include full-art seasonal Hobbit lands that are exclusive to this set, and 10 full-art Middle-Earth Journey lands (honestly, these are so cool I’d probably frame them). There’s also a die inside and a box to keep everything in.

Lloyd Coombes is an experienced freelancer in tech, gaming and fitness seen at Polygon, Eurogamer, Macworld, TechRadar and many more. He's a big fan of Magic: The Gathering and other collectible card games, much to his wife's dismay.

articles.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Is So Phenomenally Successful Because 'It's About a Lonely Guy,' Sony Boss Says
articles.summary: With Spider-Man: Brand New Day tearing up box office records, the boss of Sony Pictures has offered his thoughts on why it’s such an incredible success.
articles.body:
With Spider-Man: Brand New Day tearing up box office records, the boss of Sony Pictures has offered his thoughts on why it’s such an incredible success.

Brand New Day, which sees Tom Holland reprise his role as Spider-Man, has made over $2.4 billion at the global box office. It is the third highest-grossing movie of all time, behind only Avatar and Avengers: Endgame.

But its popularity comes not from the fact it’s a big budget superhero movie, Sony Pictures chief Tom Rothman said, as reported by Variety . It’s down to the fact that it is, essentially, a movie about “a lonely guy.”

Spider-Man: Brand New Day - Our Biggest Burning Questions

If you’re one of the few who hasn’t seen Brand New Day yet, it picks up years after the events of 2021’s No Way Home, and shows Peter Parker struggling to cope with the absence of his friends and loved ones following Doctor Strange’s memory wipe spell. A decent chunk of the first act of the movie is spent showing Parker’s inner turmoil and, yes, his extreme loneliness, which is fueled by the end of his relationship with Zendaya’s MJ.

This, Rothman insisted, is the key to Brand New Day’s appeal.

Brand New Day is “not so much a superhero film, but a super-person film,” he said. “The reason that movie has resonated all around the world is because it’s about a lonely guy… It’s like yeah, it’s about friendship. It’s very human. It’s very emotional. It’s got plenty of whiz-bang, but that’s not what the secret is. The secret is it’s a relatable story that almost everybody has related to.”

Warning! Spoilers for Spider-Man: Brand New Day follow…

By the end of Brand New Day, Peter Parker looks like he’s on the way to rekindling his relationships with both MJ and Jacob Batalon’s Ned Leeds, although the extent to which this is possible with Strange’s spell still in place remains to be seen. Certainly, Parker is in a better place at the end of Brand New Day than at the start, having also helped Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey work through her own issues.

Where does Spider-Man go from here? Given the money the movies make, there will surely be more to come. Holland himself has spoken about potentially passing the baton to Miles Morales , a character who now seems certain to be introduced into the MCU sooner rather than later.

Meanwhile, Brand New Day’s box office success continues. Will it crack $1 billion domestically? It’s on $923 million right now, so it’s certainly possible.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct — Everything Announced by Nintendo
articles.summary: It’s almost time for The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct, and IGN will be reporting live with all the news, trailers, and whatever else Nintendo has in store for us right here.
articles.body:
Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct focused on the Ocarina of Time remake, but also touched on the upcoming live-action Zelda movie. Here's everything announced.

Highlights included the first gameplay reveal for Ocarina of Time , as well as a release date. We also got confirmation of The Legend of Zelda Switch 2 Special Edition Console and Pro Controller , which look set to fly off the shelves.

There was disappointment, though, around the live-action The Legend of Zelda movie. While we did get confirmation of its title and a logo , there was no debut trailer, as fans had hoped. Given the movie itself is due out in April, hopefully it won't be long before we get a look at it.

Nintendo Switch 2: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Console Images

In case you missed the Direct, all the announcements are below. And once you're done there, let us know what you think of Nintendo's Zelda reveals in the comments.

The Zelda Direct is over, and now we know what to expect from the Ocarina of Time remake. It's clear now that this is a faithful remake that follows the original closely. Yes, there are some significant gameplay changes that will make it play more like a modern action adventure game, but all the characters, environments, and even puzzles are instantly familiar. The new visuals will, I'm sure, be the biggest talking point coming out of this Direct.

New The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake trailer

The Direct ended with the debut trailer for the remake, which began with Link riding Epona out on Hyrule Field. We then see Link running around various environments made famous from the original game, fighting various enemies, throwing bombs, and solving puzzles. We also hear fully voiced characters during cutscenes, including Ganon. The trailer ends with Young Link obtaining the Master Sword. November 5 isn't far away!

Meanwhile, Nintendo confirmed that the first print run of the physical version will commemorate the release with special packaging that features textured foil cover art, available while supplies last.

Adventure through Hyrule and become the Hero of Time when The Legend of #Zelda : Ocarina of Time releases Nov 5 on Nintendo Switch 2. #NintendoDirect pic.twitter.com/rW3r7o2L9r — Nintendo of America (@NintendoAmerica) September 8, 2026

Adventure through Hyrule and become the Hero of Time when The Legend of #Zelda : Ocarina of Time releases Nov 5 on Nintendo Switch 2. #NintendoDirect pic.twitter.com/rW3r7o2L9r

Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda - 40th Anniversary Edition

Nintendo confirmed the Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda - 40th Anniversary Edition and the specially designed Pro Controller and carry case, launch on October 29. These are going to be hugely popular!

🙌 A Nintendo Switch 2 specially designed for The Legend of #Zelda 40th Anniversary is coming Oct 29! Plus, a special Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller and carrying case are also releasing Oct 29. 👀 #NintendoDirect pic.twitter.com/ZKMniD8DEO — Nintendo of America (@NintendoAmerica) September 8, 2026

🙌 A Nintendo Switch 2 specially designed for The Legend of #Zelda 40th Anniversary is coming Oct 29! Plus, a special Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller and carrying case are also releasing Oct 29. 👀 #NintendoDirect pic.twitter.com/ZKMniD8DEO

Nintendo is also releasing two ocarinas later this year: a playable version and an electric version from HORI that plays notes or entire songs at the press of a button.

Nintendo will release Young Link as well as Young Zelda amiibo, which unlock special in-game masks "that evoke a retro graphical style," in 2027.

Several new features will be added to Zelda Notes, the accompanying app. Currently, the service supports the Nintendo Switch 2 Editions of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, but support for Ocarina of Time will help players track their adventure, challenge them to find in-game locations using hint images, let them play a virtual ocarina, and take a daily quiz with over 2,000 total questions.

LEGO The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time – Link & Epona set

Nintendo confirmed the LEGO The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time – Link & Epona set, a 1,750-piece collectible display model for adults, available starting spring 2027. Also on the way is the Hasbro Legend of Zelda Electronic Master Sword, 27 inches long with more than 15 touch- and motion-activated sounds, arriving in spring 2027.

Ocarina of Time remake release date confirmed

Ocarina of Time remake launches exclusively on Switch 2 on November 5, 2026. Take that, GTA 6!

Ocarina of Time remake gameplay and details revealed

Eiji Anouma, producer of The Legend of Zelda series, talked about the Ocarina of Time and its upcoming remake. Anouma played the remake, showing off gameplay for the first time. The action began in Kokiri Forest, showing the new art style. Link meets up with Saria, his childhood friend. There's plenty of new dialogue so the characters' personalities "shine much more."

Link can now jump at the press of a button, even in places with gaps (you couldn't do this in the original Ocarina of Time, which would make Link automatically jump when you approached the edge of a platform). Link can swim now, too.

In the shop, Link can buy Deku Nuts, as in the original game. Delving deeper into the forest, Link comes up to the Great Deku Tree, the guardian spirit of Kokiri Forest (fans of Ocarina of Time will know what happens here). Inside we see familiar gameplay, including target-based combat. Link throws a Deku Nut to stun an enemy before hitting with the sword, just as he could do in the original.

60 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 Screenshots

Deeper in the dungeon, we see a treasure chest with the Fairy Slingshot inside. All the sounds and audio effects are as they were in the original game. You can swap between items with a single button in the remake, and you can aim quickly. Remember shooting the eye with the slingshot to drop the ladder? Yep, it's still here, in the remake. There's a loading screen when you move between areas, which Anouma said Nintendo intentionally kept to preserve the feel of the original. Not sure about that one, Nintendo...

Outside in Hyrule Field is the Threads of Time feature, which is brand new. This tells you your progress in the story and your current objective. It also includes a tapestry which you fill in as you go. Off Link goes to Hyrule Castle to see Princess Zelda. In the original, Link rolled around to move faster. Now, you can hold to roll and dash, which is recommended for traveling long distances. So, yes, Link can sprint!

Hyrule Castle Town is now in third-person (in the original the camera was fixed in a top-down perspective). You can chat with all the familiar characters and their dialogue looks pretty much the same. New details were added (some that were just in the background in the original game). In the original, time stopped when you were in a town, but in the remake it continues, so you'll see the sun going down.

The Ocarina is also used to change the time of day, but in the remake you can hum a song Link has learned into the Switch 2's built-in microphone and he'll play it in the game. Yes, you, the player, can hum audio, which is turned into the song in the game. Don't pretend like you've never hummed a Zelda tune before!

Anouma said the characters Link meets are fully voiced in in-game cutscenes, which is a big change. It doesn't sound like Link talks though.

Koji Kondo took to the stage to announce Zelda concerts

Koji Kondo appeared during the Direct to talk about the music of The Legend of Zelda. The composer described how the technology behind the series' music has evolved over the years. The opening arrangment we heard at the start of the Direct was made specifically for the 40th anniversary, and includes a medley of various songs.

Concerts to mark the 40th anniversary are on the way, starting in Japan in January before heading west later in the year.

The Legend of Zelda movie name confirmed

The title of the movie is, simply, The Legend of Zelda. It doesn't have a subtitle; Miyamoto said when you see it next year you'll understand why. It sounds like it'll tell an original story that reflects the entire series, rather than a particular video game story. "This original film is based on the stories, ideas and concepts of The Legend of Zelda that have built up through 40 years of games," Miyamoto said, adding: "It's become an artistic work worthy of The Legend of Zelda series." The Triforce will play a role in the film, he teased. No trailer unfortunately, but we did get a logo.

It’s official! The live-action film of The Legend of Zelda, currently in production, will be titled The Legend of Zelda. The film is planned to be released in theatres worldwide on April 30, 2027. #TheLegendofZeldaMovie #NintendoDirect pic.twitter.com/z1sH9DXzkK — Nintendo of America (@NintendoAmerica) September 8, 2026

It’s official! The live-action film of The Legend of Zelda, currently in production, will be titled The Legend of Zelda. The film is planned to be released in theatres worldwide on April 30, 2027. #TheLegendofZeldaMovie #NintendoDirect pic.twitter.com/z1sH9DXzkK

Developer legend Shugeru Miyamoto talked about the launch of The Legend of Zelda back in 1986, and how it evolved over time. He namechecked Breath of the Wild, which ventured into "open-air exploration." He ended his message by thanking fans for their support, and to set up a reveal of the live-action Zelda movie...

The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct has begun with a nostalgic look back at past Zelda games alongside a fresh recording of the series' wonderful music performed by an orchestra. 40 years of Zelda... All in the feels!

We're only 10 minutes away from Nintendo's Zelda Direct. Hold tight, and stick with us for live reporting and reaction.

This is your 30 minute warning! We're close to kick-off time for all things The Legend of Zelda, and excitement is certainly building. If I had a Master Sword at home, I'd hold it aloft! What are you hoping to see from Nintendo today?

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Valheim Is Finally Out After More Than Half a Decade, a Breathtaking Survival Game That Stands Among the Absolute Best of the Genre
articles.summary: This is the oath of the ultimate survival crafting adventure fulfilled and carved into the very bones of the Earth.
articles.body:
In the calming meadows where my journey in Valheim began almost six years ago, at the start of an Early Access expedition that has now finally come to an end, I came across a runestone in a lonely field bearing words I've been thinking about ever since:

A full belly A full sail The weight of a spear to your hand And a song on your lips Let all the mountains crumble And the seas boil to salt One day in the sun is a life well-lived

This is the essence of Valheim, the grim-eyed but warm-hearted Norse king of survival crafting games. For as harrowing as its dark dungeons and challenging bosses may be, and unforgiving as its extreme environments of fire and ice may seem, it's a saga about returning home with chips in your shield and blood on your face to sit around a roaring hearth fire – in contemplative solitude or with friends – and feel a bright stirring in your heart, knowing that you have conquered great foes and may now rest and revel. And in those slower moments I came to realize that this was truly the best the genre has ever been.

Valheim's art direction and world design give it a distinct identity from moment one. It has a deliberately lo-fi look with pixelated textures and not a lot of polygons to go around. But even so, it's truly a beautiful game. Every creature, sunbeam, and forested hillside is filled with a sort of fairy tale ambience that made me want to get lost in its procedurally-generated regions. And there's a lot to get lost in, from peaceful meadows to dreary swamps to snowy mountains. Every time I generated a new map, it impressed me with its scale and how it looked like it could’ve been hand-made. Because of the naturalistic, Northern European feel, it comes across as very cohesive and authentic.

The first time Valheim really made me go "Wow!" was when, after about 15 hours of preparing, I set sail on my own hand-built ship. Like a proper viking, your main method of long-distance travel is to take to the seas and riverways. The controls for steering are kind of clunky, and I love them for that very reason. Mastering the art of making tight turns and managing my speed was a satisfying skill-building exercise.

Realistic waves can bounce you up and down, and a sudden storm can even damage your vessel and force you to make for a safe harbor. The ever-changing direction of the wind is a constant consideration that may encourage you to go out of your way and discover something new rather than simply sail in a straight line. Having a ship makes it feel like a whole new world is opening up – and then it tries to eat you.

The improvements to Valheim since its Early Access launch are really too many to list, even if you gloss over the obvious stuff like nearly doubling the number of biomes and bosses. Perfect dodges, trinkets, and even a magic system have made combat so much deeper and richer. One of my biggest complaints back in 2021 was that certain elements of progression could feel a bit grindy. But even that's adjustable now with fine-tuned difficulty settings. I found that a 3x resource drop rate made the pacing incredibly smooth for me as a solo player (especially while I was retreading the early areas I had already seen on an entirely fresh 1.0 world), though it might be a bit too much for a big group.

Each of the eight biomes is extremely distinct in terms of vibes, enemies, and geography. The bug-infested Mistlands have taken the place of the Swamps as my least favorite, with obnoxious terrain made even harder to navigate by dense fog, but they are beautiful to look at when you're not being swarmed. The Ashlands represent a dramatic escalation that really sells the thrill of entering the endgame with a jump in difficulty and foreboding volcanic landscapes.

As for the Deep North, I don't want to spoil too much of what secrets lie beyond its icy shores, but it really puts the ambition of all the other biomes to shame and leads into a conclusion worthy of a viking hero. I already loved Valheim's Norse aesthetics, and the Deep North is the most Norse it ever gets, so it really leans into its strongest visual and mythological themes right at the end.

For a game that already felt fairly complete in terms of both size and polish half a decade ago, Valheim 1.0 seems more like an instant classic from years back that's gotten three big expansions already, not a saggy skeleton of something that had the potential to be great that is now finally fleshed out. I feel completely spoiled by its finished scope. They've even added some really well-animated 2D cutscenes that play after each boss and announce the biome you're about to explore, which definitely help flesh out and keep up the momentum of the unfolding story.

Valheim's action hacking and slashing (and shooting) was familiar and invigorating to me as a modern action RPG player. It's not just "good enough for a survival crafter," either, with the same care and attention paid to it as any other system. With a wide variety of weapons and enemy types, elemental damage and resistances, and timing-based dodges and parries, it kept challenging me to sharpen my skills and learn new enemy patterns right to the end.

The satisfying, hectic, dramatic boss fights really demonstrate the strengths of this combat, even though it's occasionally obvious that their AI can't quite cope with the varied arenas you fight them in. Not only do they serve as climactic capstones to each area and tier of technology, they have highly distinct mechanics and gradually raise the skill ceiling needed to progress, which I found very rewarding. I do wish fully half of them were not resistant to pierce damage, though, since it feels a bit like saying, "No archery allowed past this point," especially with how long it takes for bow-wielders like me to get any significant upgrades to elemental damage in the mid-to-late game.

The randomized dungeons are also a treat, from werewolf-infested frozen cave systems to gooey insect hives, with each featuring a unique layout, loot, and challenges to navigate. The Plains and the Ashlands replace underground lairs with large, complex outdoor structures, which even further helps to keep things feeling unique. Laying siege to a charred fortress made the whole exploring and looting routine feel brand new again, even 80 hours in.

Among Valheim's most clever tricks is how your hearty feasts tie directly into progression. While you can skill up in different weapons and abilities, like running and swimming, your health and stamina meters are completely tied to what's in your belly. This means that "leveling up" mostly involves finding new ingredients and learning new recipes to ensure you're always as well fed as you can be. Valheim also wants you to eat a balanced diet. You can benefit from up to three types of food at any time, but stacking more than one of the same thing gives you no benefit.

All of this also made my character feel more alive and connected to the world, and it set Valheim apart from the rote, old-fashioned RPG progression routines where experience translates to levels, which then translate into more hit points and energy. There's something deliciously thematic about heading out to battle evil with a full stomach, a good night's rest, and a flagon of invigorating mead to quaff. It's a truly cozy warrior's paradise.

Of course, a cozy warrior needs a cozy hall to settle down in. Valheim is voxel-based, but it's also much more limited in how you can alter the terrain than something like Minecraft. It took me a while to master the little tricks needed to make a structure that doesn't clip into the ground or look like it's slightly floating. But once you do, you can construct some very impressive-looking stuff, and the in-depth system for weight and support beams means your buildings generally end up looking and feeling realistic and in keeping with the world around them. Far from a restrictive annoyance, I loved how this became like a puzzle that made me think the way actual medieval Norsemen might have when figuring out how to hold up a towering roof.There are plenty of different styles of building pieces as well, but I still wish we could get triangular or rounded floor tiles so it wasn't so hard to build something with anything but a perfectly rectangular footprint.

articles.summary: Cult classic Donnie Darko is returning to movie theaters nationwide in a restored 4K format to celebrate the film's 25th anniversary.
articles.body:
Donnie Darko will return to theaters – and in 4K – for its 25th anniversary.

Writer-director Richard Kelly’s 2001 cult classic will hit theaters nationwide on “Donnie Darko Day,” a three-day event running from October 2-October 4, 2026.

“In collaboration with American Cinematheque at the Aero Theatre and presented by Saga Arts, the special anniversary release also includes an exclusive introduction from Richard Kelly before the movie exploring the film’s enduring legacy and how it has captivated audiences for 25 years,” according to the official announcement.

Tickets are now available . Further details can be found at Fathom Entertainment’s site .

“Fathom Entertainment is thrilled to bring back Donnie Darko to theatres this fall for its 25th anniversary. This was not a film that exploded overnight - it found its audience slowly, and then never let go," said Shannah Miller, Vice President of Marketing at Fathom Entertainment.

Jake Gyllenhaal portrays the title character, who the 25th anniversary release announcement reminds us “doesn’t get along with his family, teachers or classmates, but he finds a kindred spirit in Gretchen and guidance from a compassionate psychiatrist who believes hypnosis may unlock hidden truths. Meanwhile, Donnie is haunted by Frank, a mysterious giant bunny only he can see. When a jet engine crashes into his bedroom and narrowly misses him, Donnie is drawn into a series of increasingly strange events that seem governed by forces beyond explanation.”

The movie boasts a stellar cast that also includes Jena Malone, Drew Barrymore, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Patrick Swayze, Noah Wyle, Mary McDonnell, Katharine Ross, and Seth Rogen.

IGN hailed Kelly’s film as “one of the most extraordinary directorial debuts in years, and a truly original, visionary piece of filmmaking” in our rave Donnie Darko review from 2001.

Kelly recently revealed that he’s written a Donnie Darko book sequel that will be published later this year.

Donnie Darko has made it onto several IGN lists over the years, including our picks for 10 mind-bending movies like Inception , the 15 best sci-fi movie soundtracks , the best movies that made the least money , and, yes, the 10 most famous movie rabbits .

articles.title: SteelSeries’ pro-grade, wireless Xbox controller sure is expensive
articles.summary: The $259.99 Aeon Pro is available now, and works with Xbox and PC. It includes swappable batteries, and a wireless base station to charge them.
articles.body: SteelSeries is a household name for many gamers, but not when it comes to controllers. Instead of easing into the conversation with reasonably-priced console and PC controllers to build trust, it’s kicking down the door with the $259.99 Aeon Pro wireless controller for Xbox and PC, which is now available. What does one of the most expensive controllers out there do that others don’t? A few things. The one you’ll likely notice first is its tiny OLED screen that can guide you through swapping between Xbox, PC, or Bluetooth. It lets you adjust most settings on the controller, including genre-based presets. You can remap the controls and adjust rumble sensitivity from the controller, too, but more complex stuff, like adjusting stick deadzones and making profiles, requires the GG app for PC. Screens on controllers isn’t a new concept, but this one is at least easy to use. Its most appealing feature is the most practical one: its swappable battery system. It ships with two batteries, and they last for roughly 12 hours each. The spare gets charged in the included wireless base station (it’s actually the same battery used in the high-end Arctis Nova Pro, Omni, and Elite headsets). The station has two USB-C inputs, one for Xbox and another PC. It can automatically swap sources, though you can manually swap from the controller, as well. [Image: The base station can charge a spare battery, though it’s disappointing that there’s only one right way to insert it. There aren’t a ton of other surprises with the Aeon Pro’s hardware compared to other pro-grade controllers. It has Hall effect joysticks and triggers, and most of its inputs have mechanical switches instead of membranes, yielding a more tactile sensation and sound than the standard Xbox controller, among others. And it has two-position trigger stops that let you opt for shorter throws, changing the seamless analog pull into something that feels akin to a mouse click. On its back, there are four rear paddles. They aren’t removable, which SteelSeries says is because modular ones often result in wobbly paddles. They’re just there, whether you use them or not. Like other buttons, these can be mapped through the controller, or through the GG software on PC. [Image: [Image: I like SteelSeries’ swappable battery system, and it’s great to see it come to more peripherals than just its high-end headsets. However, I’m not sold on it (or even the OLED screen) being compelling enough to warrant upgrade for if you’re smitten with your current Xbox or PC controllers. Also, at this price there really ought to be a zip-up case included, but there isn’t. For those who are wondering about alternatives, Valve’s $99 Steam Controller is a more highly customizable option for PC players. The Sony DualSense Edge is $60 cheaper and has solid PC support, too. Even on Xbox, there’s no shortage of cheaper, yet highly capable options. 8BitDo’s Ultimate 3E is $149.99 (not cheap!) yet it matches many of the Aeon Pro’s features, but with modular button sets and extra d-pads included, to boot. Still, for a company that I felt had next to no credibility in the controller space, the Aeon Pro suddenly earned it a place in the conversation. Next, let’s have a PlayStation and Switch variant. articles.title: The Legend of Zelda Live-Action Movie Will Be an Original Story Based on the Series So Far
articles.summary: Nintendo has discussed further details of its live-action The Legend of Zelda movie, including its title and story.
articles.body:
Nintendo has discussed further details of its live-action The Legend of Zelda movie, including its title and story.

Revealed during today's The Legend of Zelda-dedicated Nintendo Direct by Shigeru Miyamoto, we learned that (unsurprisingly) the film's title will be: The Legend of Zelda. Why isn't there a subtitle? Miyamoto said that when we watch the movie, we'll find out.

As for the film's story, Miyamoto said that it would be based on stories and concepts from the franchise so far. In other words, don't expect this to be a direct adaptation of a particular game. Otherwise, details on the movie remain thin on the ground (and sadly, there's no sign of Tingle just yet).

60 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 Screenshots

"The title is... The Legend of Zelda," Miyamoto said. "Once you see the film, you'll understand why there isn't a subtitle. This is an original film based on the many stories, ideas and concepts of the series, built up through the games for 40 years. Through the creative power and visual expertise of the talented production team, it's become an artistic work worthy of the Legend of Zelda series. Both the development team at Nintendo and I are also involved, of course!

"When we talk about The Legend of Zelda, there's the Triforce," Miyamoto went on to tease. "What role do you think it'll play in the film? We'll share more details at a later time, so please look forward to it."

Originally announced in 2023, The Legend of Zelda is helmed by Maze Runner and Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes director Wes Ball, while Nintendo's legendary Shigeru Miyamoto is listed as a co-producer, alongside Marvel production veteran Avi Arad. The movie was shot last winter in New Zealand, with the Middle-earth-like location now doubling for Hyrule.

The Legend of Zelda is currently set to arrive on April 30, 2027.

articles.summary: Nintendo has announced a release date and revealed gameplay for its Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2.
articles.body: Link’s next adventure now has a release date. During a Legend of Zelda stream for the franchise’s 40th anniversary, Nintendo announced that the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 is launching on November 5th. The release date makes Ocarina of Time one of just a few big-budget titles launching in the same month as Grand Theft Auto VI. Nintendo first teased the remake in June, though it didn’t reveal much aside from a brief trailer. Today’s event provided a clearer glimpse at how the company is approaching remaking one of its most influential games and the first 3D Zelda adventure. The updated version of Ocarina of Time will be the first Zelda release that’s exclusive to the Switch 2, and longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma described the remake as “a faithful interpretation using modern technologies.” The gameplay shown at the event revealed much more detailed graphics compared to the N64 original — including an intimidating take on the Great Deku Tree and a surprisingly fancy hat for Link — along with free camera movement. Other new features include something called “threads of time,” which makes it easier to see where (and when) your next destination is, and the ability to hum tunes in the game instead of playing them via the controller. Also: Link can jump now when you press a button. articles.title: Manx ferry return further delayed by 'complex' repairs
articles.summary: The Steam Packet says "complex repairs" are needed and an investigation is underway into the cause.
articles.body:
The Isle of Man's flagship ferry will be out of action for a further two months, the Steam Packet Company has confirmed, while specialist repairs take place.

The Manxman has been in dry dock in Liverpool since 13 July for scheduled maintenance.

The ferry firm said extensive wear was discovered after the shafts were removed for inspection. An independent investigation has been launched into the cause.

The back-up passenger vessel Ben-my-Chree will continue to operate services between the island and Lancashire while the work is carried out.

The update comes after a series of delays to the ferry's return , originally due to be operational again in July, and then later in September.

The operator described the refitting of the bearings and propulsion shafts, each weighing more than 17 tonnes and measuring 18 metres, as "highly complex".

Once completed, it said the process will be followed by testing, sea trials, and regulatory inspection before the vessel can resume sailings.

Managing director Brian Thomson said: "We recognise the frustration this outage has caused and sincerely apologise to our customers.

"Safety is our highest priority and Manxman will return to service only when all work is complete and fully tested. We are confident in the revised timeline announced today."

The Steam Packet said passengers with affected bookings would be contacted directly and offered alternative arrangements.

It’s not exactly a surprise to see Nintendo’s new remake get two amiibo of its own, but it’s certainly still the kind of thing fans will want to keep an eye out for in the months ahead. While we wait to see everything they’ll be able to add to the experience, you can see new screenshots below.

articles.title: Zelda Notes App Will Add a Playable Ocarina, In-Game Stats, and More for Ocarina of Time Remake
articles.summary: Nintendo's Zelda Notes app is expanding for the remake of Ocarina of Time, adding a playable Ocarina, in-game stats, and more.
articles.body:
Nintendo's Zelda Notes app is expanding for the remake of Ocarina of Time , adding a playable Ocarina, in-game stats, and more.

During today's Zelda-centric Direct , Nintendo said the Zelda Notes app is expanding to add a bunch of new features unique to Ocarina of Time. Zelda Notes was previously introduced as a companion app for the Switch 2 versions of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, but it's getting a big update for the remake.

The app will include a stat tracker which will give you daily stats based on recent play sessions of Ocarina of Time, informing you of how many enemies you have slain and more. It will also add a playable ocarina that you can use directly from your mobile device, allowing you to even compose your own scores you can share via a QR code. There's also a Zelda quiz that features over 2,000 questions.

Perhaps more notably, Zelda Notes will also add a feature that allows you to use hint images on your device to track down a hidden quest in-game. All of this is completely optional, but will enhance the experience for players who decide to get involved.

Highlights from the Zelda Direct included a The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake release date , which puts it near the blast radius of GTA 6. Of course, GTA 6 isn't launching on Switch 2, so we're talking about two different audiences. Nintendo, clearly, isn't worried about Rockstar's behemoth.

Additionally, Nintendo revealed a pair of amiibo for Ocarina of Time remake , allowing fans to collect figures of young Zelda and young Link for unique in-game items. In case you missed it, here's everything announced at The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct .

articles.title: Four Hours Is More Than Enough Time to Spend With Elon Musk, But the New Documentary Musk Should’ve Been More Comprehensive
articles.summary: Four hours is more than enough time to spend with Elon Musk, but Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk should’ve been more comprehensive.
articles.body:
This review is based on a screening from the Venice Film Festival. Musk will be released in theaters on October 16.

I like a long movie. Give me five hours of Russian journalists talking and I’ll gladly take six more , but if someone balks at the idea of spending 225 minutes (plus intermission) with Elon Musk — one of the world’s most off-putting celebrities — I couldn’t blame them. Directed by Alex Gibney, the documentary Musk is a wide-spanning exposé of things already known about the South African business magnate, who casts a long shadow on American politics. The film is certainly watchable; Gibney is a pop filmmaker after all, and this would make for great distraction when viewed in several parts, after scrolling through your streaming service of choice.

If you’re aware enough of global power players (or really, just online enough), then little in Musk will surprise you. However, the effects of seeing this much about the man laid end-to-end can be quite unsettling. So, Gibney and editor Michael J. Palmer deserve kudos for assembling a documentary epic that is — despite its lack of novelty — never boring. Although it eventually takes its subject to task over his troubling views and ventures, the film is surprisingly balanced, and gives Elon his flowers for achievements in electric cars and space exploration, up to a point. This helps answer a question Gibney poses in the opening minutes, about how so many people could become ensnared by his cult of personality, especially for someone with the charisma of a damp towel.

Elon himself declined to be interviewed; in fact, an early moment depicts a Twitter exchange where he turns Gibney down, but the director is not deterred. To retain his subject’s presence in a thematically fitting way — given Elon’s involvement in A.I. and his proclivity for wondering if we live in a simulation — Gibney’s team creates a hand-crafted digital avatar of the SpaceX CEO, with all the uncanny ugliness of an A.I. generated monstrosity (even though it isn’t one). This digital golem, who appears as though Musk had entered an arcade game and got trapped there, speaks lines from a database of everything the man has ever publicly said.

This flourish is not dissimilar to Rodney Ascher’s A Glitch in the Matrix , which builds digital representations of interviewees who believe they’re living in a computer — only in Musk, Gibney spends far less time on this and other individual conspiracies. Beginning with Elon’s early successes (as an investor, rather than an inventor), the film makes clear how he usurps companies before claiming them as his own, often stripping them for parts. Its initial hour is surprisingly nuanced for a figure either reviled or worshipped, with a fair amount of paternal backstory that explains at least some things about him. However, it soon gets into the weeds of why Elon is so downright weird, by way of interviews with several exes, and women with whom he’s fathered children.

Gibney is usually adept at deconstructing both famous figures and fanaticism. His works like Going Clear and The Inventor get to the root of how Scientology leaders and Silicon Valley swindler Elizabeth Holmes could ensnare so many, while his other film from this year, the Sundance premiere Knife , carefully peels back the zealotry that led to the stabbing of Salman Rushdie. Each of these films is incredibly accessible. Although the same is technically true of Musk — which treads subject matter similar to all three — it doesn’t feel nearly as exacting or comprehensive, despite its nearly four-hour runtime.

Chapter by chapter, the movie re-constructs Elon’s journey en route to billions in his pocket, dozens dead from self-driving automobile incidents, and eventually, a seat at the table next to U.S. President Donald Trump, with whom we see him cut hundreds of thousands of government jobs. Numerous interviews with loved ones, former colleagues and tech reporters stand-in adequately for the lack of Elon himself, whose digital avatar doesn’t add all that much beyond peripheral texture, despite being central to the movie.

It’s also unfortunate to see the movie flail when Gibney tries to re-create video game aesthetics in order to heighten and cheekily dramatize major decisions in Elon’s life. These go on a little too long and don’t have much modulation, which holds the movie back from being too provocative or subversive.

Gibney is highly aware of the radioactive personality at the center of his film, so there’s enough by way of absurd humor to counteract the unpleasantness. However, as a tale of one of the architects of our modern world, the movie’s emotional and intellectual foundation is seldom sturdy enough to stand on its own. It tends to lean on existing footage (Elon’s cameos on The Simpsons and in Iron Man 2; segments about him by comedian John Oliver and streamer Hasan Piker) to detail conflicting or evolving views in a punchy manner. It’s by no means a bad thing to pull from various sources, but each of these makes it clear that the story of Elon Musk has been told more coherently and more completely elsewhere.

Much like Elon himself, Gibney simply re-assembles existing ideas into something marketable — even though selling people on four hours on someone who comes across as a vapid, awkward huckster (with a white supremacist streak) is an uphill battle. Rare are the moments where Musk digs deep into the issues it broaches, remaining content to weave a fabric about how Elon is perceived, and will be perceived for years to come, without getting to the cultural or psychological root of why. It’s painfully ironic that Gibney’s wide-spanning documentary is unlikely to contribute to the man’s legacy in meaningful ways.

articles.title: How Star Wars Prequels and Battlefront II Influenced the Zero Company Soundtrack
articles.summary: Prolific Star Wars composer Gordy Haab reveals how his work on Battlefront II directly influenced the darker, original music for Star Wars Zero Company.
articles.body:
After nearly two decades of writing music for a galaxy far, far away, it can be argued that Gordy Haab is the most prolific composer in the Star Wars universe, John Williams included. Haab, who’s created the scores for Star Wars games including The Old Republic, Battlefront I and II, Squadrons, Jedi: Fallen Order, and Jedi: Survivor, just finished work on EA and Bit Reactor’s Star Wars: Zero Company . Now, Haab is revealing exactly how both his and Williams’s previous work directly influenced the music of the new XCOM-style game.

I sat down with Haab for an exclusive interview immediately following Star Wars Zero Company’s release, where he revealed that he considers the game’s score to be a “sequel” to other Clone Wars-era stories.

“When I wrote the score for [2017's] Battlefront II , I felt like I was really onto something. [With] Battlefront I, the assignment was to write the B-sides for the original scores. So [afterward] I really sort of branched off and started doing my own thing. So picking up [with Zero Company], I almost wanted to think of it as using Battlefront II as sort of my springboard. My parameter was ‘What would be the sequel to that?’ I wanted to have that sparkle that the Prequel era music has, but also have my personal aesthetic stamp on it.”

Haab also revealed that at a certain point after years spent working on Star Wars, he was able to throw out the Lucasfilm rule book.

Zero Company composer reveals Lucasfilm's rules for Star Wars composers

“In the beginning, Lucasfilm's direction was always ‘Be original, do your own thing, but the north star is from the original films,’” Haab says. “But then with the onset of multiple shows and games having their own original stories, that’s changed quite a bit. Each project I've worked on has had a different set of walls. When I worked on Star Wars: Hunters, I did the whole thing with an orchestra and a heavy metal band. That would not work in [Zero Company] or the Jedi series, [which is] much darker. It's much heavier, and it's got a lot of horror.”

Haab, who’s also composed music for multiple Indiana Jones games, including 2024’s Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, says he’s flattered by being associated with John Williams’s iconic music, but that the comparison does create a sense of pressure.

“In the beginning it was intimidating,” Haab says. “I felt that sort of pressure to try to live up to the original scores from the films. The ones that inspired me to even become a composer in the first place. I take those moments, I see those things happen, I absorb them, and then I quickly just forget about it and treat it as noise.

“It's almost like winning an award. I accept that award, which I consider that to be. That's a huge compliment to be spoken in the same sentence as my musical hero. But then I quickly put it away and say, ‘Don’t rest on those laurels. Do your thing, get back to work, create your voice within the franchise.’”

Despite multiple trips through the Star Wars galaxy, Haab says composing the various themes that make up Zero Company’s soundtrack presented a fresh set of challenges.

“I spent a couple months just coming up with the themes before I even started putting pencil to paper,” Haab says. “I probably wrote 15 versions of [the main] theme before I even sent it to the developers. I wouldn't even let it out the door of my own studio until I was absolutely thrilled with it. Version 1 was a lot of flourish. I spent a lot of time boiling that theme down to something that is extremely concise and simple, and I think it works.”

Haab says that, aside from the main Zero Company theme, there are two pieces of music from the game that he counts among his favorites.

Star Wars Zero Company composer reveals his favorite musical themes

“I think from a melody standpoint, [the theme for Hawks, Zero Company’s leader] is my personal favorite because it's got this heroic, drifting upwards shape,” Haab says. “[And another one] would be the theme for the Plague. I wanted it to be something [where] you could have a huge set piece with Hawks’s theme playing, and then the Plague theme would be much like the Plague itself and work its way through the texture of the music, develop[ing] into something pretty dark and heavy and grotesque.”

Haab, who says he’s been a Star Wars fan since seeing the original trilogy in theaters, revealed that there are two particular themes from those films that consistently serve as an influence for his work.

“The Force theme,” Haab says. “I think there's an obvious reason for that. It's utilized in every single one of the films and repeated multiple times. That was such an impactful moment in time for me because I was just a kid watching Luke look out over the double sunset and hearing that horn solo. I remember that, before I knew a thing about music, it shaped who I was. I think that is one of the greatest themes ever written.

“[Also], if you look at the Imperial March, the first section is very singable. Once you get into the B section of that thing, it starts to go really angular and chromatic to the point where, if you were to challenge me to sing it note for note right now, I probably wouldn't nail it. But I can remember the outline of it. I can remember the contour and the shape of it.”

After numerous accolades, including a Grammy for his work on Jedi: Survivor , Haab says that he’s eager to continue working on the franchise but that he realizes he’s just one artist in the vast Star Wars galaxy. When I asked Haab his advice for future Star Wars composers, he revealed a few key rules.

“I would say the two things that you really must take away from it are the importance of theme and not abandoning the sophistication and harmonic complexity that's available to you with a full symphonic orchestra,” Haab says. “I think that is sort of the recipe for good Star Wars music. Now what you do with it is completely up to you. Paint anything you want and it'll feel right as long as those things are honored.” Star Wars Zero Company is available now on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

For more on Star Wars Zero Company, read our 9/10 review and find out why we call it "an excellent tactical game that does a fantastic job of slathering on the same cinematic look and feel we saw in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi games."

articles.title: Doctor Strange: Endless Nightmare Preview - Experience the Lovecraftian Side of the Marvel Universe
articles.summary: We've got an exclusive preview of Doctor Strange: Endless Nightmare, a psychedelic journey into the Lovecraftian side of the Marvel Universe.
articles.body:
Abrams ComicArts is debuting the latest in its ongoing MarvelArts series of original graphic novels. This time, the focus is on the Sorcerer Supreme as he battles foes both iconic and obscure in Doctor Strange: Endless Nightmare.

With Doctor Strange: Endless Nightmare in stores now, IGN can exclusively debut a new preview of this epic, psychedelic graphic novel. Check it out in the slideshow gallery below:

Doctor Strange: Endless Nightmare Preview Gallery

Doctor Strange: Endless Nightmare reunites the creative team behind Dune: The Official Graphic Novel , including writer Kevin J. Anderson and artists Raúl Allén and Patricia Martín. Here's the official summary of the book:

When Stephen Strange encounters a mysterious patient at his hospital who won’t stop raving about how life is “nothing but the dream of a sleeping god,” the rest of the world is suddenly struck with insomnia. In order to prevent chaos from unfolding as the people around him become more and more desperate for sleep, Doctor Strange must embark into the mind of the madman who seems to have heralded this disaster, taking a psychedelic trip into the Nightmare Realm.

“The character of Doctor Strange has access to so many bizarre realms, I wanted to introduce him to a dark and twisted Lovecraft-inspired story.” said Anderson in a statement. “I brought in an important and popular villain in the Doctor Strange universe, as well as another villain who has never appeared since Stan Lee and Steve Ditko created him in 1964’s Dr. Strange #122. It was amazing to play in this universe.”

articles.title: The White House pulls its racist Tetris clone
articles.summary: The White House has removed its racist Tetris clone “Build the Wall” days after launching its “arcade.”
articles.body: The White House has taken down its racist Tetris ripoff days after launching a website dedicated to “arcade games,” as spotted earlier by Kotaku. The Tetris clone, called “Build the Wall,” involved stacking different-sized blocks to prevent a “zombie border siege.” It’s not clear why the White House removed the title, though the Tetris Company previously said that it’s looking into the situation. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy,” Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca told The Verge last week. “The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible. We are currently reviewing the matter.” The Verge reached out to the Tetris Company with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back. Other “games” that align with President Donald Trump’s agenda are still available on the White House’s website, including the Flappy Bird ripoff “Flappy Bill,” a Tapper-like game called “Supply Line,” “Trump Savings Tycoon,” and “Rio Run.”

articles.title: Practical Magic 2 Brings Back Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, But It's Cursed With a Very Messy Script
articles.summary: Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman and the rest of the Practical Magic 2 cast toil and trouble to conjure up a worthwhile sequel, but they’re cursed with a very messy script.
articles.body:
Practical Magic 2 is in theaters on September 11.

In 1998, director Griffin Dunne, along with Bullock and Kidman, delivered the equivalent of a warm autumnal Wiccan hug of a movie with Practical Magic . A modest hit at the box office, its power grew over the years as a cult favorite because of the luminous charm of the two leads as love-lorn, cursed witch sisters Sally and Gillian Owens.

Twenty-eight years later, it’s actually a little bit of Hollywood magic that Practical Magic 2 even got made with the returning cast of Bullock, Kidman, Stockard Channing, and Dianne Wiest as the matriarchs of the Owens family, all still residing together in their family home in Massachusetts. As beguiling as it is to see the return of these actresses, their alchemy is impeded by a hyperactive screenplay that’s too busy bouncing them through plot beats and muddled stakes instead of giving them, and the new cast, better stories.

Practical Magic 2 adapts from author Alice Hoffman’s novel series about the Owens clan of witches, this time primarily drawing from 2021’s The Book of Magic. It’s about 20-ish years since the end of the first film, which had the Owens witches “outing” themselves on Halloween to their little town, publicly embracing their Wiccan legacy.

Today, Bullock’s Sally is the town librarian and dedicated single mother to grown daughters Kylie (Joey King) and neurosurgeon-in-training Antonia (Maisie Williams). Because of the still intact 300-year-old Owens curse that brings death to any man to whom they confess their love, Sally has kept her girls in the dark about their magical abilities. She’s made her still free-spirited yet vaguely employed sister Gilly (Kidman) promise not to tell them, along with the reluctant buy-in of their aunts, Jet (Weist) and Franny (Channing).

But time and curses can only be held at bay for so long, and Kylie’s serious relationship with earnest Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) and the chirping of a deathwatch beetle means heartbreak and a lot of secrets are going to spill at the same time. The intersection of a curse-induced accident and Jet finding a long-hidden tome, The Book of the Raven (written by their ancestor and curse creator Maria Owens), prompts a dramatic breach in the family. A livid Kylie lays out her mother for hiding their magical abilities all their lives, and proceeds to impulsively listen to a beckoning voice compelling her to England, where it promises a way to save Gideon’s life. A road trip ensues with a panicked Sally engaging Gillian to follow, while looking up a UK expert, Dr. Ian Wright (Lee Pace), for help in unlocking the secrets of the Owens book and the history of Maria’s birthplace.

In theory, it’s not a bad idea to shake up the single locale dynamics of the first movie and dig into the family history. However, the screenplay by Akiva Goldsman, Georgia Pritchett and Kelly Marcel sacrifices the insular charm and Wiccan history of the Massachusetts community for an odd-couple travel comedy featuring the still oil-and-water sisters. Sally has been, and remains for the majority of this film, in emotional stasis, too broken and closed down from repeated losses. Thankfully, Bullock still knows how to make an audience feel the pain of her character. But there’s also a strong sense that the script is wasting the broader talents of what Bullock could have brought to her character rather than give her a one-note trajectory that you see coming a mile away.

Kidman does her impish best to play Gillian as the devil on Sally’s shoulder, trying to break those tall emotional walls while pushing her towards the very handsome and multi-tattooed Dr. Wright. But outside of playing her frustrated sister’s keeper, the script shorts the actress any parallel meaty story like she had with the murder of Gilly’s truly frightening ex-boyfriend Jimmy (Goran Visnjic) in the first film. When Bullock and Kidman get some rare quiet moments to just let the sisters talk, they make the most of it every time. But those moments are few and far between the more the chase for Kylie picks up and gets burdened with an overly convoluted exposition dump about the ancient history of the area where Maria was burned to death, and who or what has been summoning Kylie.

As for Pace, I’ll never understand how an actor as charming and compelling as he is gets handed such underwhelming material. If you can’t write a character for the man that is clearly swoon-worthy from the get-go, you’re doing something incredibly wrong. In fact, it’s a little insulting that Wright is introduced in a stunt set piece that frames him purely as eye candy, with little clarity of purpose aside from playing a potential love interest. And even then, the script gives Bullock and Pace scenes with so much tonal whiplash it’s never clear if they’re actually flirting, or just being passive-aggressive with one another. The heat and charm found between Sally and Aidan Quinn’s Detective Gary Hallet in the first film is sorely missing between Sally and Wright no matter how hard the actors try, and that's a big problem in getting the audience to buy the power of love.

The film’s other cardinal sin is separating the main cast, with Bullock, Kidman, Pace and King essentially in their own mini chase movie in picturesque, tax-incentivized England. Director Susanne Bier doesn’t frame the locations or set pieces with much scale or even the fairy-tale charm that Dunne shot the first film with, so the sequel lacks the mood and menace that gave the original such memorable vibes. Meanwhile, Channing, Williams and Maridueña are stuck back home in what feels like a single-room loaner hospital set from a soap opera. In particular, Williams is done dirty, given nothing of note to do, which is a travesty. Ageism also looms with Weist and Channing, who are relegated to cliché fates that work as well as they do only because of both women’s immense talent for wringing the most out of any scene they appear in.

I was also particularly disappointed that Alan Silvestri’s score from Practical Magic, so essential in creating the tone of the original, is only gently alluded to in Rupert Gregson-Williams’ original score. Instead, Bier and company lean on other nostalgic reprises that just don’t have the same weight or impact as Silvestri’s themes.

Though Practical Magic 2 isn’t a terrible second chapter, one is left at the end with the feeling that a much better sequel, with more deeply considered and well-crafted versions of the Owens women, might be floating somewhere out there in the winds above Massachusetts.
